item.title: Mesoporous Separator Engineering Rectified Electrolyte Chemistry for Durable Non-Aqueous Aluminium-Ion Batteries
item.description: Rechargeable non-aqueous aluminium-ion batteries (AIBs) are promising low-cost and sustainable energy storage systems, but their development is hindered by sluggish transport of strongly associated chloroaluminate ions and unstable aluminium plating/stripping. Here we demonstrate that engineering the separator microenvironment effectively regulates electrolyte chemistry and interfacial ion transport in AIBs. A binder-free dendritic mesoporous silicamodified glass fiber (DMS-GF) separator is developed by growing DMS nanoparticles directly 2 at the GF scaffold surface. The resulting silanol-rich mesoporous architecture weakens anioncation interactions in chloroaluminate electrolytes, promotes ion dissociation, and shifts electrolyte speciation towards the electrochemically active Al2Cl7 - species, leading to enhanced ionic mobility. The interconnected mesoporous channels further homogenise ion transport and electrolyte distribution, enabling highly reversible and stable aluminium plating/stripping with suppressed dendrite growth. In graphene//Al full batteries, the DMS-GF separator enables high reversible capacity, improved rate capability, and long-term cycling stability, outperforming pristine GF separators. This work demonstrates that separator microenvironment engineering can synchronously regulate electrolyte chemistry and interfacial electrochemical processes for high-performance AIBs, providing a promising strategy for controlling ion transport in unconventional battery systems.

item.title: Orbital-Optimized Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory Within the Tamm-Dancoff Approximation Using Lagrangian Minimization
item.description: Time-dependent density functional theory in the Tamm-Dancoff approximation (TDDFT/TDA) is a computationally tractable approach for calculating excited electronic state energies and properties. TDDFT/TDA constructs single-excitation electronic states from Kohn-Sham molecular orbitals where the occupied orbitals have been variationally optimized according to the Aufbau principle and the virtual orbitals are left unrelaxed. To investigate the effects of incorporating state-specific orbital relaxation into the single-excitation determinant, a Lagrangian-based state-specific orbital-optimization (OO) method is derived where stationarity of a targeted TDDFT/TDA Lagrangian with respect to orbital rotations is enforced using the analytic orbital-rotation gradient. Rigorous test calculations on vertical excitation energies across valence, Rydberg, fluorescence, and charge-transfer (CT) excitations spanning configuration interaction singles (CIS), global hybrid, and range-separated hybrid functionals reveal distinct functional-and state-specific trends. Specifically, OO-CIS improves 75.6% of singlet valence excitations relative to conventional CIS. For CT excitations, the range-separated hybrid rCAM-B3LYP yields a significant improvement, reducing the mean absolute error by 0.233 eV, whereas other global and range-separated hybrid functionals show less improvement or worse performance. Furthermore, for some transitions orbital optimization can significantly underestimate excitation energies, revealing critical challenges when relaxing orbitals in the TDDFT/TDA framework.

item.title: End-to-End Learning from Experimental Data: Integrating the PC-SAFT Equation of State into Neural Network Training for Improved Polymer Parameter Estimation
item.description: Accurate and computationally efficient thermodynamic models are essential for the design, optimization, and operation of many (bio)chemical processes involving polymer solutions, blends, and membranes. In this work, we combine machine learning (ML) with the PC-SAFT equation of state (EoS) to predict the non-associating pure component parameters for polymers, enabling the rapid evaluation of the pressure–volume–temperature (PVT) behavior of polymer melts and rubbers. Using a dataset of more than 5,400 PVT measurements for 78 chemically diverse polymers, we systematically evaluate the effects of EoS integration in the training process, the molecular representation, neural network architecture, and transfer learning. A baseline approach trained on pre-fitted PC-SAFT parameters is compared with a physics-informed approach that embeds the EoS in the training loop, enabling end-to-end training directly on experimental PVT data. Performance is assessed using 6-fold cross-validation. For a feed-forward neural network (FNN) using extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs), embedding the EoS reduces the average mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 8.67% to 5.57%. Replacing the FNN and ECFP representation with a graph neural network (GNN) using cyclic polymer graphs further reduces the average MAPE to 2.58%. Pre-training the models on PC-SAFT parameters for small molecules, followed by fine-tuning on polymer PVT data, yields additional improvements, reducing the average MAPE to 5.06% for the FNN and 2.15% for the GNN. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining an embedded EoS with geometric deep learning and transfer learning for accurate polymer PVT predictions.

item.title: nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT: Spin-complete mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT with a noncollinear exchange–correlation kernel
item.description: We present nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT, a spin-complete mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT with a complete noncollinear exchange–correlation response. The theory unifies the two extensions of MRSF-TDDFT, the noncollinear kernel of nc-MRSF and the spin-complete closed–virtual (CV) space of CV-MRSF, in a single response operator. Three parameter-free rules supply every density-functional interaction that the completed CV space requires: the transverse kernel is added wherever exact exchange acts, the Coulomb interaction of a singlet-coupled CV pair is completed with its longitudinal kernel, and the semilocal spin potential enters one-electron elements as its spin average. As a result, the response yields spin-pure states, is covariant under separate closed, singly occupied, and virtual orbital rotations, and recovers the isolated Tamm–Dancoff excitation matrices of a closed-shell fragment separated from the reference open shells, which triplet-pair degeneracy alone does not ensure. With 20–25% exact exchange, nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT gives lower Thiel singlet and triplet errors than either parent method. At this common optimum of nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT and conventional TDDFT for singlet excitations, the singlet excitation energies of the two methods are comparable, while the B1LYP singlet–triplet gap MAEs on Thiel and QUEST are 71–77% lower with nc-CV-MRSF-TDDFT than with conventional TDDFT in the RPA or TDA. However, the principal advantage of the method lies beyond vertical excitations: as a spin-complete mixed-reference response that treats ground and excited states on an equal footing, it is expected to carry this accuracy into strongly correlated regimes where single-reference TDDFT fails, including diradicals, bond breaking, doubly excited states, and conical intersections.

item.title: How Chemical Evidence Shapes Mechanistic Reasoning and Prediction by Large Language Models: Fine-Grained Inference in Nucleoside-Derived Supramolecular Gelation
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) offer a distinctive capability for chemical problem solving by integrating chemical knowledge and experimental evidence through reasoning expressed in natural language. Yet how chemical evidence reshapes their predictions and expressed rationales is not self-evident and has received limited examination, particularly for challenging chemical problems. Here, using nucleoside-derived supramolecular gelation as a testbed, we systematically varied the evidence provided to LLMs and quantitatively evaluated their predictions and the mechanistic alignment of generated rationales. Without additional evidence, correct predictions were associated with greater alignment to literature-supported mechanisms than incorrect ones, suggesting that LLMs can draw on intrinsic chemical knowledge despite rationales remain largely general. Structurally similar gelation precedents, thought improved prediction accuracy significantly, reduced this distinction by anchoring rationales to insufficiently discriminative structural features, indicating that similarity-based evidence does not necessarily improve chemical reasoning and that prediction accuracy alone is insufficient to assess LLM performance in chemical tasks. In contrast, condition-constrained references and mechanistic information more consistently directed rationales toward chemically discriminative features, even when prediction accuracy did not improve in tandem. Together, our study highlights the importance of task-specific evidence design and quantitative rationale evaluation for reliable chemical problem solving by LLMs.

item.title: The Multi-Objective Computational Design and Prioritization of Novel TSPO PET Radioligands for Improved Inflammation Imaging after Traumatic Brain Injury
item.description: Clinicians employ TSPO PET imaging to quantify the extent of TBI-associated neuroinflammation through radioligands that bind to the central pocket of the human translocator protein. However, many radioligands underperform due to pocket dissociation and low blood-brain barrier permeability. I hypothesize that a targeted cheminformatic pipeline can accelerate the pre-synthetic design of novel TSPO ligands with improved physicochemistry. Eight second-generation ligands were benchmarked using preclinical physicochemical and PET metrics. Emapunil was selected as the modifiable scaffold. Haloalkylation was curated across two functional groups, establishing a 1922-analog dataset. Following prioritization based on molecular descriptors and docking energy, 15 lead candidates (assigned IDs of A#) proceeded to PBPK modeling. Leads were z-scored, and the top three candidates advanced to plasma-input Logan analysis. Consensus ADMET prioritized leads for short-timescale molecular dynamics. The top four analogs were evaluated through a five-replicate 10-ns MD panel along with the reference, and retrosynthetic routes were devised through ASKCOS. A7 showed a significantly improved static and dynamic profile over emapunil. A7 displayed a 5.4-fold increase in partition coefficient and fourfold increase in brain-plasma concentration ratio in the PBPK simulations versus the reference. Logan VT slope estimates were stable for A3, A6, and A7. MD showed A7 retained 28.25±5.94 mean fixed-pocket contacts and ≥10 contacts in 97.96±2.04% of frames. A7’s contact advantage over AC-5216 was statistically significant after Holm correction (p=0.0317). ASKCOS predicted 200 complete synthetic routes for A3, A8, A15, and emapunil with buyable terminals, while A7 displayed an unresolved N-difluoromethylation terminal. Pareto analysis identified A7 as the only nondominated analog. A7 emerged as the strongest radioligand candidate and demonstrates the effectiveness of a cohesive cheminformatic system in PET radioligand development.

item.title: IRexp: A database of experimental infrared band lists from open-access literature
item.description: Machine-learning models for infrared (IR) spectroscopy are often trained on computed spectra, yet simulated spectra differ from measured ones, and large, open experimental IR datasets remain scarce. Here, we introduce IRexp, an open collection of 230,946 experimental IR band lists (cm⁻¹ peak positions) extracted from 19,859 open-access articles published between 2005 and 2026 and their supporting information, together with an author-entered Chemotion repository deposit. In total, 96,973 records are linked to a resolved structure, and 50,682 of these also carry author-reported ¹H and ¹³C NMR. Record quality was checked manually against the source documents and by automated consistency tests. IRexp holds more than four times as many experimental IR records as existing public IR spectral libraries, and every record keeps its source identifier and licence, with records released in licence-specific files. We expect IRexp to accelerate data-driven IR spectral prediction, automated structure elucidation, and multimodal models trained on real experimental data.

item.title: Matched Metal–Organic Frameworks Reveal How Chemistry and Pore Structure Shape Gas Adsorption
item.description: Designing metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for adsorption requires distinguishing pore-chemistry associations from differences in architecture. An outcome-independent matched-comparison analysis of the ARC–MOF v7 simulation database pairs frameworks with identical topology and dimensionality and closely constrained values of seven pore descriptors. The resulting 13,072 chemistry-changing pairs are benchmarked against similarly matched pairs with unchanged represented chemistry labels. Across 18 gas–temperature–pressure states, linker-family changes exhibit the most consistent adsorption separation beyond this empirical background, whereas coordination-compatible metal substitutions show more context-dependent behavior. Residual-geometry adjustment attenuates the linker-associated contrast by approximately 36–40% under the primary linear specification and 20–27% under the tested additive nonlinear specifications, while retaining an overall positive linker-associated signal. These model-dependent estimates do not identify a causal contribution from pore geometry. Uptake differences frequently contract at higher loading and need not translate into favorable working capacity or selectivity. Structure-resolved comparisons and common-protocol RASPA simulations reveal strong, near-null, and electrostatically sensitive cases without constituting independent experimental validation. The analysis establishes structurally matched observational comparisons as a practical route to interpretable chemistry–structure–adsorption relationships and helps prioritize follow-up modeling and measurement.

item.title: Assessing the transfer-learning performance of foundation models for energetic materials property prediction under low-data conditions
item.description: This study evaluates the performance of off-the-shelf foundation model embeddings provided by CheMeleon, MolCLR, and MACE-OFF to predict energetic material properties from sparse datasets. Models were trained to predict crystal density, heat of formation and impact sensitivity from SMILES strings, with performance benchmarked against molecular representations provided by Morgan fingerprints and hand-crafted descriptors. Overall, the foundation model embeddings were found to be competitive with the hand-crafted descriptors, with MACE-OFF showing the strongest performance in numerical regression tasks. Heat of formation was found to be the most predictable property (R2 = 0.72), followed by crystal density (R2 = 0.54) and impact sensitivity (R2 = 0.47). Testing under more demanding cluster-based data splitting revealed that MACE-OFF retained the strongest performance across representations, suggesting that its learned embeddings generalise more effectively than hand-crafted descriptors to molecules that are more dissimilar to the training set distribution. Predictability for impact sensitivity improved noticeably when recast as a classification task, where CheMeleon emerged with comparable performance to the hand-crafted descriptors. These results show that while foundation model embeddings can provide useful low-input screening tools for energetic materials, they are not yet a competitive replacement for the bespoke models trained on larger datasets.

item.title: A Novel Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7// Li4Ti5O12 Dual-Ion High Power Battery
item.description: Concerns over lithium abundance and safety have driven the search for alternatives to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are promising owing to sodium’s abundance and low cost, but sluggish Na+ diffusion and limited rate capability hinder their practical use in high power batteries. Here we report a mixed (Li/Na)-ion battery as a low-cost, high-power alternative solution. We demonstrate a novel mixed-ion Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7(NFPP)//Li4Ti5O12(LTO) full cell operating in a lithium-based electrolyte with excellent performance. The cell delivers an average operating voltage of 1.9 V, an initial capacity of 109.6 mAh g-1 and 80% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 1C, along with exceptional rate performance maintaining discharge capacities of 87.3 and 73.5 mAh g-1 at 10C and 20C, respectively. The results show that both electrodes undergo reversible Li+/Na+ co-intercalation via the Fe2+/Fe3+ (NFPP) and Ti3+/Ti4+ (LTO) redox couples. The cathode incorporates Li, reaching Na2.64Li1.16Fe3(PO4)2P2O7 at initial full discharge, while Na uptake into LTO is lower (Na0.87Li6.12Ti5O12 at initial full charge), as revealed by In-situ X-ray diffraction, ICP-OES and XANES. The long-term cycling stability, and high-rate capability, demonstrate NFPP/LTO as a high power, long-life Na/Li mixed-ion battery and provides new insight into mixed-ion charge-storage mechanisms to direct future research in this area.

item.title: Resin 3D Printing with Dose-Controlled Solubility
item.description: Vat photopolymerization (VP) offers high resolution and throughput with low surface roughness, but requires support structures that limit printable geometries, generate non-recyclable waste, and must be removed manually. We introduce dose-controlled selective solubility vat photopolymerization (dSSVP), wherein a low 405 nm light dose forms linear acrylate chains, while high doses deplete a base quencher and initiate cationic epoxide polymerization to form a solvent-resistant crosslinked network. Raman spectroscopy and cure depth measurements quantify the cure kinetics and inhibition period before epoxide polymerization begins. After printing and heat treatment, low-dose regions dissolve rapidly in food-safe solvents, while high-dose regions resist dissolution and exhibit a bending modulus of ≈3 GPa. A variety of complex demonstration prints are presented, including a dental aligner, an MIT “Brass Rat” class ring, and an assembly of interlocked parts. Further advancement of dSSVP could enable fully automated production of finished parts using widely available single-resin desktop VP hardware.

item.title: Plasma-Enhanced Surface Doping SnNiOx Nanofilms for Water Oxidation
item.description: The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) limits the efficiency of alkaline water electrolysis, and the rational design of non-precious-metal anodes requires an understanding of how a dopant modifies an oxide surface. Although atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs) offer high intrinsic activity, precise synthesis and characterization of their local active sites remain challenging. Surface doping provides a tractable alternative for probing intrinsic activity and correlating it with the dopant coordination environment. Here we use plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PE-ALD) to deposit sub-monolayer doses of Fe and Co on ultrathin SnNiOx films grown on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO). item.title: From Divergence to Coupling: Interfacial Water and Adsorbed Hydrogen during Hydrogen Evolution
item.description: The structure of interfacial water is widely invoked to explain the kinetics of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet how it evolves relative to adsorbed hydrogen (H*) and responds to changes in electrode potential remains unclear. Here, we simultaneously track interfacial water and H* on platinum during potential pulses using Dynamic Response Spectroscopy (DRS), which separates interfacial-and diffusion-layer contributions to the measured spectra. As the potential is lowered from 0.4 VRHE, we identify three potential regions, defined by the dominant interfacial processes and characterized by different relationships between water and H* dynamics. In the hydrogen underpotential deposition region, where H* adsorption dominates, H* follows each potential step, whereas interfacial water restructures progressively over the first cycles and does not recover its initial configuration. At 0 VRHE, where hydrogen adsorption and evolution are in equilibrium, water follows each potential step but continues to relax during holds at constant H* coverage. Under net HER, water and H* evolve in concert. These results show that hydrogen coverage alone does not determine the dynamic state of interfacial water. Rather, their dynamic coupling depends on the dominant interfacial process, highlighting the importance of interfacial history when interpreting spectroscopic measurements of electrocatalytic interfaces.

item.title: Reticular Programming of Gold Nanocluster Electronic States Enables Near-Unity Faradaic Efficiency in Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electrosynthesis
item.description: Achieving selective nitrate-to-ammonia electrosynthesis requires more than accelerating nitrate activation: the catalyst must sustain eight-electron reduction while preventing premature intermediate release and competing hydrogen evolution. Yet controlling these competing processes through the molecular architecture surrounding well-defined metal centers remains challenging. Here, we report the first application of gold nanocluster covalent organic frameworks (COFs) to electrocatalytic nitrate-to-ammonia conversion, establishing reticular connectivity as a strategy for programming catalytic electronic environments. Four crystalline frameworks (KIN-1–KIN-4) were constructed from a common pyrazolate-bridged Au3 cluster and structurally differentiated organic linkers. Despite preserving predominantly Au(I) centers, the frameworks exhibit distinct frontier electronic-state distributions, pore architectures, and electrochemical selectivities. The triformylphloroglucinol-linked KIN-2 delivers a near-unity ammonia Faradaic efficiency of 99.5% at −0.70 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, with an ammonia productivity of 0.75 mg h-1 cm-2 and only 0.8% Faradaic efficiency toward nitrite. Isotopic labeling verifies nitrate-derived ammonia formation, while in situ attenuated total reflectance surfaceenhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy and differential electrochemical mass spectrometry reveal evolving reactionassociated signatures. Density functional theory identifies preferential *NO hydrogenation through *NHO rather than NOH, with respective uphill free-energy increments of 0.66 and 1.36 eV, alongside unfavorable hydrogen adsorption (ΔGH* = +1.62 eV). These findings demonstrate that reticular construction can differentiate reaction energetics without changing the metal’s formal oxidation state, offering a molecular design principle for directing multielectron electrocatalysis toward desired products.

item.title: Short-circuit-resistant sulfide solid-state batteries through lithium dewetting
item.description: In sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries, lithium dendrites penetrate the solid electrolyte indiscriminately through grain boundaries, interparticle voids and pores, causing internal short circuits that accelerate degradation and terminate cell life. This penetration has been understood largely in mechanical terms, and mitigation has focused on suppressing cracks. Here we show that chemical wetting, governed by the lithium/electrolyte interfacial energy, is a decisive factor in lithium penetration. Even when crack pathways were mechanically suppressed, short circuits persisted, because the negative interfacial energy renders sulfide electrolytes lithium-wetting, drawing lithium into their pores. Incorporating a small amount of tungsten, which strongly repels lithium, induced lithium dewetting and suppressed infiltration. The resulting electrolyte sustained lithium plating and stripping for more than two years without short circuiting and enabled long-lived high-rate full cells and anode-less pouch cells under low stack pressure. These findings establish interfacial energy as a key design parameter for durable all-solid-state batteries.

item.title: Multilevel Reproducibility Assessment of Polymer Monolithic Capillary Columns for Peptide Separations
item.description: Polymer monoliths have emerged as attractive stationary phases for peptide and intact-protein analysis, offering an alternative to packed-bed columns. Their synthesis involves several critical manual steps raising concerns about reproducibility and transferability of the synthesis protocol. This study systematically evaluates the robustness and reproducibility of an established synthesis protocol where two operators synthesized two of column batches of 100 µm i.d. poly(styrene-co-divinylbenzene) monolithic capillary columns and assessing their performance in peptide separations. Column robustness was investigated through 70 consecutive peptide separations performed on a representative polymer monolithic capillary column. The column maintained its chromatographic performance, achieving retention-time stability comparable to commercial packed nanoLC columns (CV < 0.5%). The within-batch reproducibility of the columns was found to be generally high, with the coefficient of variance (CV) of the pressure drop below 10% and CV of retention times and peak width below 3% and 8-15%, respectively. Multivariate testing by multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) was performed to compare batches of the same operator and columns from different operators, detecting no significant difference between the operators (p = 0.2802). Our study demonstrates the reproducibility of polymer monolith fabrication across multiple levels, establishing the robustness and transferability of the synthesis protocol.

item.title: Photoinduced Direct N-Arylation of Nitroalkanes at Ambient Temperature via 1,2-Boronate Shift
item.description: Although photoexcited nitroarenes have been explored for facile reductive couplings, owing to their higher energetic n→π* electronic transition compared to the nitroarenes, the metal-free reductive C-N coupling reaction with nitroalkane under the photochemical condition is not known. We report, for the first time, the photoexcitation of nitroalkanes and their participation in metal- and photocatalyst-free reductive C−N coupling with arylboronic acids at ambient temperature via 1,2-boronate shift. This protocol overcomes the long-standing challenge of photoexciting nitroalkanes, including nitromethane, despite their volatility and explosivity. Thus, nitromethane, widely used as a solvent, is explored as a methylamine surrogate. A series of nitroalkanes conjugated with natural products and pharmaceuticals underwent metal-free reductive coupling with boronic acids, in quantitative yields. Photophysical studies and control experiments suggest that nitroalkanes were excited to the triplet diradical state near 390 nm and then participated in electron transfer with PPh3/phosphite as the deoxygenating agents. This redox process is triggered by the formation of a thermodynamically favourable nitroso intermediate and POPh3. Subsequently, a pre-nitrene intermediate may form, which attacks the electron-deficient boron centre, followed by a 1,2-boronate shift accessing the N-arylated product. Remarkably, no external photocatalyst is required, demonstrating nitroalkane as a photosensitizer for the first time. This method is operationally simple, industrially viable and valuable for synthesizing various biologically important scaffolds and late-stage modification of the drug molecules at room temperature.

item.title: Computational Studies on the Stability of BINOL-CPA/Imine Complexes
item.description: Chiral BINOL-derived phosphoric acids (CPAs) are widely used Brønsted acid catalysts in enantioselective synthesis, where the relative stabilities of experimentally accessible binary CPA/imine complexes have been linked to stereoselectivity, yet previous quantum-chemical studies using implicit solvation showed substantial deviations from their observed E/Z ratios. Here, we combine density functional theory with explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations in dichloromethane, using quantum-chemically derived force fields together with thermodynamic integration and umbrella sampling to determine solvation and complexation free energies. For the investigated systems, the calculated free-energy differences reproduce the experimental E/Z ratios with good accuracy and quantify the relative contributions of solvation and complexation, demonstrating the value of explicit-solvent free-energy simulations for describing CPA/imine equilibria. The method also enables conformational analysis, revealing that the Z isomers access a broader range of relative CPA–imine configurations than the E isomers, suggesting an entropic contribution to their stabilization.

item.title: Pre-Nucleation Conformational Ordering Revealed by Optical Trapping Raman Microspectroscopy
item.description: During molecular crystal nucleation, solute molecules are forced to adopt positions, orientations, and conformations consistent with the crystal lattice. Although positional and orientational ordering during crystal nucleation have been extensively investigated, the evolution of conformational order remains poorly understood, despite its importance in determining crystal polymorphism. In this study, we monitored the evolution of conformational order during crystal nucleation using in situ Raman microspectroscopy combined with optical trapping. Sodium oxalate was selected as a model system because its oxalate anions predominantly adopt twisted conformations in aqueous solution but a planar conformation in the crystal. Immediately before crystal nucleation, Raman spectra revealed a gradual increase in the population of planar conformers, accompanied by a decrease in that of twisted conformers, suggesting that conformational ordering precedes crystal nucleation. This suggests that the conformations adopted in the crystal are governed by an overall energetic balance, including solute–solute interactions, rather than by only the conformational stability in bulk solution. Thus, conformational ordering within prenucleation aggregates may contribute to the subsequent positional and orientational ordering in the resulting crystal, thereby highlighting the potential importance of controlling the local solution environment to promote the formation of target crystal polymorphs.

item.title: An environment-conditioned QM/MM resource for protein–ligand electron densities and quantum-informed pose rescoring
item.description: Structure-based drug design relies on geometric and empirical features, whereas electron density encodes polarization and weak interactions but is costly to obtain at biomolecular scale. We present a multilevel QM/MM resource from MISATO trajectories and PDBbind complexes, comprising 104,636 electronic-structure records across 96,467 geometries. Physics-embedded equivariant surrogates achieve 0.326–0.384% density NMAE on PDB-disjoint tests with explicit TIP3P water; predicted receptor electrostatic potentials agree with reference values (Pearson r = 0.99529). For pose rescoring, we evaluated quantum electrostatic and non-covalent interaction descriptors on 405 four-filter generalization complexes, each with 20 poses from Vina, smina and AutoDock4, including at least one with heavy-atom RMSD <2.0 Å. Matched ablations improve Top-1 recovery by 7.41 percentage points over Vina-derived inputs and by 3.70–4.69 points over geometry-only arms. Full models achieve 69.14–70.12% Top-1 success.

item.title: Ligand Topology, Homoconjugation and Flexibility in Pyridine-Pyrrolide Tetrel(IV) Complexes Dictate Excited State Decay
Intrinsic Excitation Polarization across the Exciton Manifold of Individual Molecular Nanotubes
item.description: The polarization of excitonic transitions provides insight into molecular organization, but ensemble spectroscopy averages over many assemblies, while photoluminescence measurements at the level of individual assemblies predominantly probe their lowest-energy excitonic states. Here, we use polarizationresolved photoluminescence-excitation microscopy to probe higher-energy excitonic states in individual double-walled molecular nanotubes (DWNTs). By varying the excitation wavelength and polarization while detecting the red tail of the photoluminescence, we determine the reduced linear dichroism relative to the long axis of each DWNT and characterize the distributions of polarization directions among individual DWNTs. The lowest-energy excitonic transitions are polarized almost entirely along this axis, whereas higher-energy transitions exhibit a more complex interplay of longitudinal and transverse contributions. Selective photo-oxidation of the outer wall reveals strongly transversely polarized inner-wall excitations and exposes ambiguities in previously established assignments of higher-energy excitonic states. These findings open a route to mapping the excitonic organization of individual molecular assemblies and, ultimately, identifying microscopic structural heterogeneity that would otherwise be obscured by ensemble averaging.

item.title: A coupled experimental-modeling framework for evaluating the electrochemical performance of lithium-ion battery electrodes remanufactured with recycled LiFePO4
item.description: The rapid growth of electric vehicle and electronics markets is generating a rising volume of endof-life batteries, making recycling essential to recover critical materials and reduce environmental impact. The electrochemical performance of future recycled batteries needs to be optimized by identifying the best remanufacturing parameters. Here, we propose a coupled experimental and computational framework that moves towards this objective by using the recycling of LiFePO4 (LFP) as a proof-of-concept. We first characterized a spent LFP material, subsequently we used direct recycling to obtain a regenerated active material to remanufacture recycled LFP electrodes. We also fabricated a pristine LFP electrode reference, and blended electrode (50:50 recycled-to-pristine ratio). The three samples were characterized by various experimental techniques, including electrochemical testing, microscopy, granulometry, etc. The experimental determinations were then used as inputs to generate representative 3D electrode microstructures and parameterize a 3D-resolved electrochemical model for each sample. The models managed to simulate the galvanostatic discharge curve of the three electrode samples, capturing the experimental trends with high accuracy at C/50 and C/20 C-rates. Furthermore, we analyzed the microstructural bottlenecks and benchmarked the three LFP electrode types. Our framework introduces a chemistry-agnostic approach to optimize blend ratios in blend electrodes containing recycled materials.

item.title: The ADAPT Map: circuit rewrites and over-conjugated states in ADAPT-VQE
item.description: Variational quantum circuits are usually judged by the energy they reach. We ask by what route ADAPTVQE reaches the ground state, and follow both the optimized angles of all its circuits, tabulated as the ADAPT Map, and the bond orders of the state optimized at each depth. In three polyenes, an H6 chain, and benzene, re-optimization hardly changes the earlier angles up to a system-dependent depth. At that depth the change jumps by an order of magnitude and a generator already in the circuit is selected again with the opposite sign, while the convergence curve shows at most a change of pace. In a replay of this circuit, the first copy of the generator carries probability out of the Hartree–Fock determinant and the second carries it back. The partly applied circuit passes through states up to about 1 Eh above the Hartree–Fock energy, although the final state hardly changes. In the polyenes and the H6 chain, the operations between the copies act as spectator excitations (a single excitation plus the hop of a second electron), absent from the singles-and-doubles pool. In these four systems the double bonds are corrected early. The single bonds follow only after about 99% of the correlation energy has been recovered, once single excitations enter. In between, the states are over-conjugated, with a bond-order alternation smaller than the exact value. When chemical accuracy is first reached, it is still too small by a fifth to a quarter of its Hartree–Fock error. Benzene shows no such stage.

item.title: What we know and what we don’t: an audit of experimental solid-electrolyte data, and the patent literature as an untapped source
item.description: Machine-learning (ML) models for solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) are trained on experimental ionic-conductivity data, yet public datasets are smaller, more duplicated and noisier than their sizes suggest. We merged the five open Li conductivity datasets we could download (Liverpool Ionics, Laskowski et al., McHaffie et al., OBELiX and the text-mined set of Shon and Min) and audited them in three ways. First, after re-extracting one dataset from its PDF table, normalising compositions and collapsing copies, the four curated datasets shrink from 3,336 nominal entries to 1,481 unique compositions from 540 papers; the CSV rendering most users would download hides a fifth of them. 86% of OBELiX records are exact copies of records in its parent datasets. Second, for 194 compositions reported by two or more papers, the median spread is 3.4-fold, and a report lies on average 0.43 log units from its composition median, nearly three times the spread among eight laboratories measuring identical powder. A systematic offset per paper accounts for 85% of this between-paper variation, and phase labels explain much of the largest spreads, while activation energies vary between papers no more than between laboratories. Third, one gradient-boosting model scores a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.90 log units under random cross-validation, 1.20–1.42 when entries from the same paper are kept together, 1.89 on a time split and 2.24 when a structure family is held out, worse than predicting the median; five other learners show the same pattern. Concatenating public datasets without deduplication lets copies leak into test folds and lowers the random-split MAE to 0.57, close to the experimental spread. We also built and tested a pipeline that extracts composition–conductivity records with evidence quotes from 100 recent patents in CPC H01M 10/0562. One in five reports measured conductivities, and these documents hold 171 distinct lithium compositions, 92% of them absent from the open datasets; halides make up a third of them against 4% of the literature set, and garnet and perovskite oxides are missing. Against a 25-patent reference set the pipeline recovers about half of the table records at a precision of 0.84; the reference set was drafted by the extraction model and has not yet been checked by hand, so these scores are provisional. We recommend a minimum reporting standard for conductivity, published duplicate maps and versions for datasets, group-aware splits reported against the experimental spread, and release of patent-derived facts with citations only.

item.title: Action-Conditioned Sparse Mixture-of-Experts World Model for Predicting Microplate Observations in Robotic Chemistry
item.description: Automated chemistry requires both reaction-outcome prediction and monitoring of the physical execution of experiments. We study an action-conditioned model for predicting welllevel plate observations after robotic operations. The architecture combines address-masked action injection, sparse experts routed by a chemistry-oriented scene descriptor, and a gated pyramid decoder for local refinement. In the reported trajectory evaluation, the model reaches PSNR 29.6 and failure-detection F1 0.79 at 7.6 GFLOPs and 118 ms per plate. A separate evaluation on high-throughput reaction datasets reports yield 𝑅2 of 0.821. Because the available appearance and yield data come from different sources, these results assess complementary tasks rather than an end-to-end action–appearance–yield trajectory on the same plate. We also examine component ablations, cross-scenario behaviour and inference cost.

item.title: Deconvolution for high-resolution oversampling MALDI MSI
item.description: Decreasing pixel size is essential to resolve single cells via mass spectrometry imaging. Here, we present a bioanalytical and computational pipeline to perform oversampling MALDI-MSI from tissues and cells and deconvolve oversampled MALDI-MSI results. By comparing to histochemical staining and fluorescence microscopy, we can show that deconvolution improves the quality of resulting images compared to unprocessed MALDI-MSI data. Despite the signal loss due to oversampling compared to regular MALDI-MSI data acquisition, we can obtain 166 annotations in positive-ion mode for mouse kidney. At the same time, we show that we can visualize single cells in tissue with a pixel resolution of 600 nm, subcellular distributions in cells with down to 900 nm, and enable measurements of different tissues and cells in both ion modes. By using mouse spleen tissue and combined fluorescence microscopy, we demonstrate that we can visualize single neutrophils within spleen tissue and obtain lipid profiles for these tissue-resident single innate immune cells.

item.title: Novel Triple-action Pt(IV) prodrugs with carbocyanine and chalcone in axial position: photoactivation, tumor targeting, fluorescent tumor visualization, and high therapeutic efficacy
item.description: Pt(IV) prodrugs are highly promising platform for anticancer agents due to the ability to fine-tune the structure and properties of the prodrug by varying the axial ligand conjugated with the Pt(IV) core. In this study, we have synthesized photoactivated Pt(IV) prodrugs with NIR-absorbing cyanine and chalcone in axial positions, which combine the advantages of dual-target chemotherapy, controlled photoactivation, photodynamic therapy, and fluorescent NIR bioimaging. The cyanine-chalcone-based prodrug Pt-4 demonstrated the ability to generate ROS, release carboplatin intracellularly and promote p53 expression under 660 nm light. Pt-4 prodrug demonstrated superior pharmacokinetic properties to carboplatin and excellent fluorescent imaging of CT-26 tumors. In vivo, Pt-4 prodrug + 660 nm light stimulated adaptive immune response in LLC tumors and significantly inhibited tumor growth of homograft CT-26 tumor. Our findings demonstrate excellent potential of Pt(IV)-carbocyanine light-activatable platform for tumor imaging, drug delivery and tumor eradication.

item.title: Efficient, Repeatable and Cost-effective 17O-Isotopic Labeling of Proline and Hydroxyproline for 17O-NMR Analyses
item.description: L-Hydroxyproline and L-Proline are two amino acids commonly found in proteins, and which are also used for making cocrystals of pharmaceutical interest. Understanding their local environment and dynamics at the atomic scale using techniques like solid-state NMR is thus of interest. Here, we propose cost-effective and repeatable synthetic strategies to label in oxygen-17 the carboxylic group of these amino acids, and of their Fmoc-derivatives. The labeling procedures, some of which involve mechanochemistry, are described in detail, and the 17O solid state NMR spectra of the enriched materials are reported. In the case of L-proline, variable-temperature measurements were performed, showing the presence of dynamics within the crystalline phase.

item.title: Cobalt Isolated Single-Atomic Sites for Iso-butane Direct Dehydrogenation with Robust Anti-Coke Deposition
item.description: Developing efficient, coke-resistant catalysts based on earth-abundant metals remains a major challenge for the direct dehydrogenation (DDH) of light paraffins, a reaction commonly catalyzed by costly Pt-based catalysts. Herein, we report a catalyst featuring isolated single-atom Co sites (Co ISASs) that achieve 46% isobutane conversion and 90% selectivity to isobutene at 550 °C. The catalyst maintains stable isobutene selectivity throughout a 24 h stability test, with no coke deposits detected by high-resolution transmission electron microscopy or Raman spectroscopy. Theoretical calculations suggest that single-atom Co sites favor isobutene desorption over further dehydrogenation, thereby suppressing coke precursor formation and providing a mechanistic explanation for the observed coking resistance. These findings highlight isolated Co sites as promising non-noble-metal catalytic centers for selective, coke-resistant isobutane dehydrogenation.

item.title: A Multi-Gram Synthesis of 7,12-Dibromo[7]helicene
item.description: Functionalized helicenes offer a concise synthetic entry to chiral optoelectronic materials. Despite the relevance of these building blocks, the structural diversity of known difunctionalized helicenes remains limited, reflecting the synthetic challenges associated with specific substitution patterns. Herein, we report a 10-step synthesis of hitherto unreported 7,12-dibromo[7]helicene in multigram quantities. A single Mallory photocyclization was employed at a late stage, harnessing the bromine substituents as blocking groups to achieve regiocontrol. An inefficient and throughput-limiting Mallory reaction at an early stage of the synthesis was circumvented by accessing the key tetrasubstituted phenanthrene precursor through intramolecular carbenoid coupling. The entire route was repeated multiple times and independently reproduced by different chemists, with the majority of compounds isolated without chromatographic purification.

item.title: Position-Dependent Conformational Landscapes of Flavin–Tryptophan Pairs in Designed Magnetosensitive Protein Maquettes
item.description: Photoinduced electron transfer is a fundamental mechanism in biological energy transduction and signal processing and can generate spin-correlated radical pairs whose subsequent reactivity is modulated by external magnetic fields. Elucidating how the local molecular environment governs the formation and dynamical evolution of such radical pairs remains a major unresolved problem, particularly in biologically relevant settings where multiple electron transfer pathways may operate concurrently. Rationally engineered flavomaquette constructs offer a tractable system for interrogating these nonequilibrium electron transfer phenomena within a reduced and well-defined molecular framework. In prior studies, placement of a single tryptophan electron donor at three distinct positions along a flavin-functionalized peptide helix produced substantial variations in photochemical outcomes and magnetic-field sensitivity that are not accounted for by the nominal donor–acceptor distance alone. In the present work, we examine the molecular determinants underlying these differences using atomistic simulations of three flavomaquette variants—W13, W16, and W20—in both their neutral and charge separated states. Despite a shared fourhelix scaffold, the simulations indicate that the constructs support markedly different spatial organizations of the redox active moieties. Specifically, W13 predominantly populates conformations characterized by close flavin–tryptophan contact; W16 samples both compact and more extended geometries; and W20 preferentially adopts widely separated configurations. Comparisons between independently sampled neutral and charge separated ensembles further show that the electronic state of the redox centers modulates the conformational landscape accessible to the donor–acceptor pair and alters the energetic response of the surrounding molecular environment.

item.title: MIRAL Cloud: Integration and Orchestration for AIEnabled Experimentation
item.description: AI-enabled automated experimentation combines experimental platforms, analysis tools, and robots to support high-throughput screening and adaptive experimental decisions. These capabilities often rely on independently developed software, creating a need to coordinate execution while preserving the scientific context of results. We present MIRAL Cloud, an integration and orchestration system developed for the Material Innovation through Robotics and AI Laboratory (MIRAL) at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. MIRAL Cloud exposes specialized laboratory capabilities as reusable operations within a shared workflow environment while retaining local instrument and procedure control. Three representative use cases illustrate complementary aspects of this approach: training and workflow development on a small-scale experimental platform, adaptive dissolution in which AI-based image analysis guides conditional solvent addition, and perceptionguided robotic sample handling. Together, these cases illustrate how experimental measurements, analytical responses, and placement outcomes remain linked to their originating requests and inform subsequent workflow steps across application-controlled experiments, commercial automation, and robotic operations. A browser workspace supports workflow configuration, execution monitoring, and inspection of results alongside supporting observations and source records. The contribution is a shared integration approach for coordinating heterogeneous capabilities within MIRAL, with reusable operation descriptions, connectors, and linked scientific records providing a basis for adaptation to other automation laboratories.

item.title: A Stereocontrolled Synthesis of (4R)-1-Methyl-4-Propyl-L-Proline, the Amino Acid Fragment of Lincomycin
item.description: We present a concise route for the stereoselective conversion of commercial (cis)-4-hydroxy-L-proline into (4R)-1-methyl-4-propyl-L-proline, the amino acid fragment found in the clinically used antibacterial antibiotic lincomycin. Our account of success is accompanied by a discussion of two failed routes. The rise of antimicrobial resistance necessitates the continued search for new antibacterial agents.

item.title: [HYD-Py]3: light- and acid-driven reversible in-plane ring breathing between physicochemically and functionally distinct expanded and contracted states of an 18-membered nonaazamacrocycle
item.description: Stimuli-responsive macrocycles can alter shape through conformational reorganization or changes in covalent connectivity, but repeatable, connectivity-preserving resizing of an intact ring has remained elusive. Here we report [HYD-Py]3, an 18-membered nonaazamacrocycle that undergoes reversible in-plane ring breathing while preserving atom count and bonding topology. Condition-selective divergent cyclotrimerization of a bifunctional pyridine monomer furnishes expanded all-trans and contracted all-cis states, the latter locked by a cyclic array of three intramolecular N–H···N hydrogen bonds. Irradiation drives contraction via sequential C=N isomerization within the intact macrocyclic skeleton, whereas trifluoroacetic acid disrupts the hydrogen-bond network and restores the expanded state, enabling repeated cycling. Ring breathing reconfigures cavity size and surface polarity, producing distinct solubility, fluorescence, self-association propensities and π-surface recognition; the expanded state also functions as a multidentate metal-ion receptor.

item.title: Clarifying BBL's Folding Mechanism: Non-Cooperative, Barrierless Folding from Enhanced MD and Chemical Shift Analysis
item.description: Accurate structural characterization across thermal folding/unfolding transitions is essential for understanding protein folding mechanisms. Here, we combine extensive molecular dynamics simulations with LEGOLAS, a fast and scalable machine-learning-based NMR chemical shift predictor, to map the complex folding landscape of BBL, the peripheral subunit-binding domain from Escherichia coli 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (PDB: 2CYU). BBL has two stable helical regions (referred to as helix 1 and helix 2), linked together by a very flexible region. Using temperature replica exchange molecular dynamics (T-REMD) in explicit solvent from 200 to 500 K and analyzing almost 64,000 conformational snapshots, we reveal non-cooperative folding of BBL's two-helix architecture. Conformational clustering was followed by ensemble-averaged 𝐻!, 𝐶! , 𝐻", N NMR chemical shifts predicted using LEGOLAS. Thermodynamic curve fitting shows marked differences in helix stability: helix 1 exhibits greater thermostability (𝑇#= 388 ± 31 K, ΔH0f = 13 ± 3 kcal mol-1) compared to helix 2 (𝑇# = 334 ± 22 K, ΔH0f = 9 ± 4 kcal mol-1). Despite quantitative differences, the calculations qualitatively agree with experimental observations. This work establishes LEGOLAS-enhanced molecular dynamics as a powerful framework for dissecting protein folding thermodynamics and extracting mechanistic insights that complement experimental NMR studies.

item.title: SACred: mining the Protein Data Bank for single-atom catalyst sites
item.description: Single-atom catalysts (SACs) are built from a small set of sites, most often a metal held by four nitrogens, while enzymes run hydrogen evolution, O2 and CO2 reduction and N2 fixation on single metals in many different first coordination shells. Here we mine that diversity. SACred, an automated pipeline built and run with AI agents, reduces every transition-metal site of the Protein Data Bank (PDB) to its first coordination shell, turns the recurring shells into candidate SAC sites and screens them in a funnel: each shell is mapped onto a single or double vacancy in graphene, screened with GFN2-xTB calibrated per metal against DFT, refined with PBE-D3 DFT for hydrogen adsorption (∆GH), formation energy (Ef) and dissolution potential (Udiss), simulated at 1,500 K with a fine-tuned MACE force field and checked against the literature by agents. From 291,977 metal sites in 53,868 PDB entries the pipeline builds 1,155 graphene sites for xTB and 123 for DFT. We validate each stage. Extraction agrees with the PDB’s own metal–ligand annotation (precision 0.98, recall 0.94). The mapping keeps all donors for 98 % of the sites but distorts single-vacancy geometries. In a prospective test, sites picked by calibrated xTB reached |∆GH| ≤ 0.3 eV in DFT in 67 % of cases, against 39 % for sites picked from enzyme knowledge alone and 44 % for a random sample from the xTB window (p = 0.06 and 0.07), and the whole xTB stage cost about 400 core-hours, as much as four to five

item.title: Total Synthesis and Biological Evaluation of Cannalactone, a Noncanonical Strigolactone from Hemp
item.description: Strigolactones (SLs) are apocarotenoid phytohormones secreted by plants into the rhizosphere. They act as signaling molecules for the development of arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi. SLs also play a crucial role in stimulating the seed germination of root parasitic plants such as Orobanche, Phelipanche, and Striga, which are among the most threatening weeds to major crops worldwide. Phelipanche ramosa primarily infests rapeseed, hemp, and tobacco, with population P. ramosa 2a preferentially attacking hemp and population P. ramosa 1 targeting rapeseed. Due to their significant role in plant development, SLs have been the focus of extensive research. By isolating and characterizing SLs, researchers aim to develop methods to control parasitic plants. Recently, a novel noncanonical SL, named cannalactone, has been discovered in the root exudates of hemp. Cannalactone selectively stimulates the germination of P. ramosa 2a seeds compared to P. ramosa 1. This work describes the total racemic synthesis of cannalactone and evaluates the biological activity of cannalactone on P. ramosa populations from 3 different hosts, Orobanche minor and Orobanche cumana compared to the natural product isolated from root exudates. Additionally, a synthetic approach to a deuterium-labeled standard of this natural product has been developed.

item.title: λproc: a compositional language for process description, with a case study in chemical synthesis
item.description: Processes—cooking recipes, formulations, industrial flowsheets, chemical synthesis procedures—are recorded as prose or as diagrams. Neither form is machine-checkable, neither admits a canonical string, and neither makes the reuse of a sub-process explicit. We present λproc, a language in which a process is written as a composition of functions over streams: a unit operation is a function from streams to streams, a sub-process is a named lambda, and the process graph is not drawn but emerges from referential transparency—two textual mentions of the same expression denote the same physical node. The language is specified by a grammar of five productions, a canonical form that maps each process to exactly one string, and a validator that decides whether a document denotes a well-formed process. We argue that these three properties make λproc a useful target for machine learning, and we test the claim on a case study. Converting 1 808 937 reactions text-mined from US patents yields 700 149 distinct λproc documents and, notably, zero invalid ones: the converter either produces a well-formed process or rejects the reaction. Trained on this corpus, a decoder-only transformer of 2.73 M parameters reads a target molecule and writes a synthesis procedure that validates in 99.7 % of cases and recovers 24.5 % of the reactants of the real procedure on molecules it has never seen. It is measured against two trivial baselines, and the comparison is instructive: a nearest-neighbour lookup over 597 350 training molecules ties it on the conventional metric, and diagnosing that tie shows the metric itself to be dominated by ubiquitous reagents—a constant answer scores 0.133 on it. On a metric restricted to building blocks the lookup falls to 0.180 while the model holds 0.266. Three further results follow. The grammar saturates at the smallest model size tested, so capacity buys chemistry, not syntax. The validator makes rejection sampling exact: ten samples yield ten usable procedures, with an oracle of 0.422 against 0.260 for the model’s own ranking, but no reference-free feature we measured recovers more than 0.005 of that gap. And conditioning on an inventory of available materials triples reactant recall to 0.764, where the model selects rather than copies the shelf—but stress tests show it trusts the shelf: when the right reactants are absent it falls below the unconditioned model, and when near-miss analogues stand in for them it substitutes them inside documents that still validate. A pretrained 350 M-parameter language model, fine-tuned on the same corpus in five configurations, loses by a factor of three. All code, weights and an interactive application are released with this paper.

item.title: Mechanistic Pitfalls of Unbalanced Excited-State Descriptions across Competing Pathways: Thiophene as a Case Study
item.description: A balanced description of excited states remains challenging even for small organic molecules. For thiophene, we show that an unbalanced description can conceal an entire relaxation pathway. Comparing SA-CASSCF and RMS-CASPT2 potential energy curves toward the ring-opening (RO) and ring-puckering (RP) conical intersections, we identify the state carrying the molecule to each crossing, termed the carrier state. Dynamic electron correlation leaves the RO carrier (πσ*) state nearly unchanged but strongly stabilizes the RP carrier (ππ*) state. Consequently, the RP channel opens in RMS-CASPT2-based surface hopping simulations (26% versus 67% for RO), whereas it was absent in previous CASSCF-based ones. Through this RP channel, molecules return almost exclusively to the ring-closed form, thereby shifting the predicted photoproduct distribution toward nearly equal rearranged and ring-closed fractions. Concealment of a competing pathway is not apparent from Franck–Condon energetics alone but exposed by tracking the states along paths to the crossings.

item.title: Materials Acceleration Platform Enables Material-Efficient High-Throughput Study of n-Doped Conjugated Polymers
item.description: This paper describes a material-efficient method to evaluate the performance of n-type conjugated polymers using the RoboMapper Material Acceleration Platform across a large parameter space. We utilize the platform to investigate the n-doping of the benchmark N2200 polymer, which we synthesized in a small batch size, utilizing n-DMBI across 112 processing conditions, spanning solvent composition, dopant concentration, and annealing temperature. Material usage is reduced by 83 % compared to conventional spin-coating. We identify a maximum conductivity of 8.21 × 10−4 S cm−1, with processing conditions at 75 % chlorobenzene in o-dichlorobenzene, 25 % dopant concentration, and 140 °C annealing temperature, and achieve comparable results using large area coatings prepared by blade-coating. We characterize the doping process by UV-Vis absorbance, FTIR spectroscopy, and electrical measurements all within the same automated platform. The results are consistent with literature data and with traditional thin films, validating RoboMapper as a fast, efficient platform for evaluating milligram-scale batches of n-type conjugated polymers and dopants, without the need for manual measurements spin-coaters, or other wasteful processes.

item.title: Binding of legacy and emerging PFAS to Na-and Ca-montmorillonite basal surfaces: roles of the exchangeable cation and layer-charge heterogeneity, with implications for vadose-zone leaching
item.description: Clay minerals are widely assumed to retard per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in soils, yet the strength and mechanism of PFAS binding to smectites are unresolved: measured montmorillonite Kd values span two orders of magnitude, and the only published free-energy simulation of PFAS on smectite predicts logKd values higher than any measurement. We combined umbrella-sampling molecular dynamics of ten legacy and emerging PFAS (C4–C8 perfluoroalkyl carboxylates and sulfonates, GenX, ADONA, 6:2 FTS and F-53B) on Na-and Ca-montmorillonite with a Gaussian process regression (GPR) model of soil Kd and a vadose-zone leaching screen. On an evenly charged basal surface, binding is weak for every compound (free-energy minima between +0.6 and −9.8 kJmol−1), stronger with Ca2+ than with Na+ for nine of ten PFAS, and net exclusion from the surface occurs for six of ten PFAS on Namontmorillonite. Two independent force fields agree within 0.6 kJmol−1 for PFBS on Ca-montmorillonite, and a stiff-restraint contact test finds no deeper inner-sphere state. Concentrating the layer charge into patches deepens binding by 4 kJmol−1 for PFBS and 12 kJmol−1 for PFOS, with the molecule residing on the uncharged siloxane patch;

item.title: Non-compliant site welding of thermomechanically treated reinforcing bars: joint efficiency, failure mode and code conformance of three commercial grades
item.description: Butt-welded splices in reinforcing bars are routinely made on South Asian construction sites with general-purpose rutile electrodes, without preheat or procedure qualification. This study examines the consequences for three commercial thermomechanically treated (TMT) bars, B500CWR (10 mm), B500DWR (16 mm) and B600D-R (16mm),joinedbyshieldedmetalarcweldingwithE6013 electrodes under those conditions. The bars were characterised before and after welding by optical emissionspectroscopy,tensile,bend and rebend testing,opticalmetallography,Vickershardness traversesand scanning electron fractography.As received,allthree barsshowed the TMT casetransition–core structure and met their specified strength requirements. After welding, retention of yield strength fell from 93.6% to 87.4% to 79.4%, of tensile strength from 88.3% to 79.7% to 72.1%, and of elongation from 49.9% to 26.9% to 21.8%, in the order of carbon equivalent (0.432, 0.541 and 0.647, IIW). The weld metal was the softest region of every joint (81–87% of the base-metal hardness); the heat-affected zone softened in B500CWR but hardened to 229–240 HV in the two higher grades, without forming martensite. B500CWR passed all post-weld bend and rebend tests, and one of its joints failed in the base metal by microvoid coalescence. B500DWR passed only one of three rebend tests and B600D-R failed every post-weld test; both fractured in the weld metal by cleavage initiated at gas porosity. No joint developed the 125% of specified yield strength that AWS D1.4 requires of a direct buttsplice.Carbon equivalent,ratherthan strengthgrade,governstheresponseofTMT barsto uncontrolled site welding.

item.title: Environmental Selection of Thymine over Uracil in Prebiotic Chemical Evolution: Insights from a Kinetic Monte Carlo Model
item.description: The replacement of uracil (U) by thymine (T) is a defining chemical feature of the transition from RNA-to DNA-based heredity. While thymine’s superior stability is well known, the role of prebiotic environmental conditions in driving this selection remains quantitatively underexplored. Here we present a stochastic kinetic Monte Carlo model (UPDSF v4.4) that simulates competition between uracil and thymine across four archetypal prebiotic environments using strictly literature-derived parameters. Molecular fitness is quantified by a Stability-Kinetics Ratio (Sr = τ_stable / κ_poly). Simulations show strong, environment-dependent selection: thymine is preferentially preserved in high-temperature hydrothermal, UV-exposed, and wet-dry cycling regimes due to its enhanced resistance to hydrolysis, deamination, and photodimerization. In contrast, uracil retains a kinetic advantage in lipid-assisted cryogenic eutectic phases where concentration effects and lower polymerization activation energy favor its incorporation. These results indicate that heterogeneous prebiotic environments could have 2 imposed deterministic physicochemical filters favoring thymine in DNA precursors. The model provides a quantitative platform for integrating kinetic data into origins-of-life scenarios and highlights the importance of spatial and temporal environmental heterogeneity.

item.title: Quantifying trends across a series of leaving groups in mixtures containing ionic liquids
item.description: The nucleofugality of fluoride was measured in a range of solvent mixtures containing ionic liquids. The first order rate constants associated with the solvolysis of the fluorides of well-described electrofuges were determined in mixtures of ethanol and different proportions of the ionic liquid 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide. Temperature-dependent kinetic analyses allowed determination of activation parameters and rationalisation of observed solvent effects in different ionic liquid mixtures through consideration of solvent interactions with species along the reaction coordinate. From the solvolysis data of those fluorides, the nucleofugality of fluoride was determined in these systems. Further, the nucleofugality of fluoride was determined in mixtures containing high proportions of six additional ionic liquids in ethanol. These data allowed for quantification of the effects of varying both the amount of ionic liquid present in the reaction mixture, as well as the component ions, on the nucleofugality of fluoride. Importantly, several differences were noted in both the microscopic origin of the solvent effects and hence the nature of the effects of different ionic liquids on the nucleofugality of fluoride in comparison to previously studied halogen leaving groups, highlighting the importance of nucleofuge size and charge density in understanding the origins of the observed reactivities.

item.title: EVALUATION OF ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS, PHYSICOCHEMICAL CHARACTERISTICS, PHYTOCHEMICAL CONSTITUENTS AND GC-MS ANALYSIS OF POLYALTHIA LONGIFOLIA ETHANOL LEAF EXTRACTS
item.description: In the array of traditional medicine, Polyalthia longifolia is one of the highly esteemed plants because of its high potency for curing numerous diseases. The plant contains various bioactive compounds that promote a healthy life. Purpose: This study involves the assessment of the impact of environmental conditions on the physicochemical properties, phytochemical analysis, and the GC-MS characterization of bioactive chemicals in polyalthia longifolia leaf extracts. Design of study: The leaf sample was taken at various times, including 6:00 a.m., 1:00 p.m., and 6:00 p.m. The leaf of Polyalthia longifolia was screened qualitatively for phytoconstituents using n-hexane and ethanol extracts. Method: The extraction process involved using polar solvents, maceration for 72 hours, extracting 250 g of powdered samples, decanting, filtering, drying, concentrating, and storing the crude extract for further analysis. Results: The preliminary report of these leaf extracts confirmed the presence of these phytochemicals: alkaloids, tannins, flavonoids, steroids, glycosides, saponins, carbohydrates, and anthraquinones. GC-MS characterization showed that the most abundant compounds were found to be greater than 1%. Guaia-1(10) 11-diene at all times of harvest: morning (3.81%), afternoon (8.22%), and evening (9.52%)., followed by Spiro[5.5]undec-2-ene, 3, 7, 7-trimethyl-11-methylene- morning (3.99%), afternoon (6.76%), and evening (8.39%), followed by hexadecanoic acid, ethyl ester in the morning (4.19%), afternoon (4.81%), and evening (4.70%), respectively. Conclusion: This study suggests that P. longifolia leaf extracts are rich in phytochemicals like tannin, flavonoids, saponin, glycosides, and alkaloids and have potential as a drug source. However, further studies are recommended to determine the toxicological safety of these extracts and to investigate how time, temperature and other environmental conditions affect the bioactive compounds in this leaf.

item.title: De Novo Design of Blood-Brain Barrier-Penetrant, P-Glycoprotein-Evading EGFR Inhibitors and Hypoxia-Activated Trapping Analogs for Glioblastoma
item.description: Background: Most Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM) tumors about 50% grow because of a very overreactive protein called EGFR (Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor). Existing drugs like Erlotinib and Gefitinib work great for lung cancer, but they are not effective for brain cancer and subsequently fail for three main reasons. First, they are too water-attracting (polar, with TPSA > 74 Å2), and second, they are very heavy with a molecular weight above 390 Da. Due to all of these factors, they are unable to cross the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB). Third, even if they get inside, the brain has security systems like P-glycoprotein (P-gp), which pushes them back outside into the blood, thereby wasting their potential inside the brain. Methods: In order to solve this without the use of an expensive lab, we came up with an automated cloud pipeline on GitHub Actions in collaboration with an LLM (Google Gemini). There are four tools that we used: 1. SELFIES: A system that mutates molecules with proper valency and bonding rules to make them 100% chemically valid. 2. Adaptive Mutation Scaling (σ / sigma): A controller where small tweaks are made when improving a winning molecule, and if the molecule is stuck or not what we are looking for, it makes a bigger jump to get a new mutation. 3. XGBoost: A regressor model trained on real lab data (ChEMBL203) with a similarity guardrail. 4. 3D Protein Docking (PDB: 1M17): A 3D check to test how each molecule actually fits inside the human EGFR crystal structure for Glioblastoma. In total, we completed 1,417,569 generations and the engine tested 4,317,102 unique molecules. Results: There were five reward-hacking measures taken by the regression model and mutator, which were fixed via our iterative human-in-the-loop system: 5. Self-Training Echo Chambers: First, we stopped the AI from feeding its own unverified guesses back into its training data, because those unverified guesses were providing high score results that are practically impossible (pIC50 > 150), which is what we called echo chambers. 6. Unstable Sulfur Triple Bonds: Second, we blocked unstable sulfur triple bonds (ClS#CO...) that would attack healthy cells even though they were yielding a high score in both Blood-Brain Barrier penetration and pIC50 score. 7. Flat Double-Bond Tails Crashing in 3D: Third, we caught flat double-bond tails (=CCCO and NCCC=C1...) that looked good in 2D math but crashed into the roof (Leu694) of the 3D protein pocket, which means they cannot actually attach properly to the Glioblastoma EGFR protein. 8. Tightly Bent Small Rings: Fourth, we blocked tightly bent 3- and 4-membered small rings ([r3] and OC1=NC=C1), because carbon and nitrogen bonds naturally sit at 109.5° to 120°, and forcing them into 60°–90° angles creates severe angle strain (Baeyer strain) that makes them snap open in water. 9. Reactive Chlorine Warheads: Fifth, we filtered out toxic chlorine warheads (-CH2Cl), which are similar to sulfur triple bonds where they could actually harm healthy cells even though they provided good theoretical results. After all of these conversions and fixing these loopholes, we finally got a winner, which is Lead 1 (CCc1c(Nc2cccc(F)c2)ncnc1N1CCCO1). This engine discovered a family of compact, lightweight pyrimidine molecules ranging from 268 to 309 Da that had strong EGFR blocking power (IC50 = 5.20–6.92 nM, pIC50 = 8.16–8.28) and strong 3D binding (ΔG = -7.54 to -8.90 kcal/mol). For further verification, we tested it on the SwissADME server, which confirmed that our Lead 1 can actually cross the Blood-Brain Barrier (TPSA = 50.28 Å2), escapes the P-gp pump (P-gp substrate: No), does not block liver enzymes (CYP3A4 inhibitor: No), and has zero toxicity alerts (0 PAINS / 0 Brenk alerts). This was our result for Lead 1 after the verifications and filters that we passed all the molecules through. How It Reacts in the Body (Our Two New Solutions): When looking at how Lead 1 reacts in the body, we came across two solutions that address the whole problem: 10. The "Trojan Horse" Trapping Mechanism (Lead 1 → Lead 1-M): Basically, Lead 1 has a closed 5-membered ring (N1CCCO1) with a weak nitrogen-oxygen (N–O) single bond that hides its polar charges (HBD = 1, TPSA = 50.28 Å2) so it can sneak across the Blood-Brain Barrier. Because its polar charges are masked inside this closed ring, it easily sneaks across the Blood-Brain Barrier and enters an oxygen-starved (hypoxic) brain tumor. Once inside, the reductase enzymes present in the tumor cut the weak N–O bond open, which releases -36.40 kcal/mol of energy (MMFF94s) and turns it into another molecule that we named Lead 1-M (CCc1c(Nc2cccc(F)c2)ncnc1NCCCO — where "-M" stands for the active ring-opened Metabolite of Lead 1). item.title: Tailoring Amorphous Solid-state Electrolytes through Inorganic Crosslinking
item.description: Amorphous solid-state electrolytes (a-SSEs) are promising for all-solid-state batteries, but their synthesis remains empirical because network formation is poorly understood. Inspired by step-growth polymerization, we describe mechanochemical a-SSE formation as inorganic crosslinking, in which lithium-salt anions link metal-halide centers through precursor activation, oligomerization, network crosslinking, and kinetic arrest. Com- bining atomistic simulations with di!raction measurements on ZrCl4 paired with seven lithium salts, we identify the anionic linker as the central synthetic variable. Linker geometry determines whether the product crystallizes or remains amorphous, sets the connectivity of the resulting network, and thereby shapes the local Li+ coordination environments that govern transport. Networks that favor chloride-only Li+ coordination conduct fastest, reaching room-temperature conductivities of order 1 mS cm→1 or higher. These findings connect precursor chemistry to network topology and ion transport,

item.title: Modeling IR and VCD Spectra of L-Phenylalanine Polymorphs with Polarizable Force Field Molecular Dynamics
item.description: Building on the computational framework developed by Bowles et al. [J. Chem. Phys. 158, 094305 (2023)] for IR and VCD spectroscopy of alanine in the gas and condensed phases, we employ a polarizable AMOEBA-based approach to investigate solid-state vibrational spectra. We investigate the vibrational properties of two distinct L-phenylalanine (Phe, C9H11NO2) polymorphs: the anhydrous Powder form and the hemi-hydrated Fiber structure. Phenylalanine forms complex crystalline architectures stabilized by extended zwitterionic (−COO− · · ·−NH+ 3 ) hydrogen-bonding networks, whose influence on vibrational properties remains challenging to characterize. We demonstrate that polarizable molecular dynamics simulations provide an effective approach for reproducing the solid-state IR and VCD spectra of these polymorphs. While the IR spectra exhibit largely similar features, the VCD spectra show pronounced differences between the Powder and Fiber forms, providing a sensitive spectroscopic fingerprint of their distinct supramolecular arrangements. These results highlight the enhanced sensitivity of VCD to intermolecular effects and crystal organization and establish polarizable molecular dynamics as a promising approach for characterizing structural polymorphism in molecular crystals.

item.title: Electrochemistry in air enabled by electric-field spillover at three-phase interfaces
item.description: Electric-field spillover at dielectric/electrolyte/electrode interfaces drives electrochemical reactions in traditionally forbidden environments, including insulating liquids and gases. Here, we show that ferrocene present in either air or toluene undergoes concerted electron- and phase-transfer at the molecularly thin 3-phase boundary, resulting in its oxidation and the transfer of the reaction product, ferrocenium, into the aqueous phase. A detailed investigation of the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of these reactions reveals that concerted electron- and phase-transfer in air proceeds substantially faster than in the liquid dielectric, toluene. These remarkable differences are the result of smaller solvation constraints, shorter electron-tunneling distance, stronger electronic coupling, and faster diffusion of reactants. Our findings establish electrochemistry in air as a platform for rapid interfacial reactions.

item.title: RGST-ΔSCF: Response-Guided Construction and Tracking of Excitation-energy-Resolved states along surface Reaction Pathways
item.description: Illumination can promote or inhibit catalytic reactions, yet the origin of their excitation-energy dependence remains unclear. Here, constrained ΔSCF calculations and spin- and k-resolved wavefunction-overlap tracking are used to follow nonequilibrium electronic configurations across four excitation-energy intervals along H2-dissociation pathways at doped Cu/ZnO interfaces. The preferred pathway switches from final-state-referenced configurations at low excitation energies to initial-state-referenced configurations at higher energies, with dopant-dependent crossover energies and nonmonotonic barrier responses. Metal-site dopants regulate reactivity primarily through excitation-induced reconstruction of collective metal-H bonding, whereas support-site dopants act through pathway-dependent interfacial spin redistribution. Neither excitation energy nor the magnitude of charge, bonding, or spin redistribution alone universally predicts catalytic promotion; the response depends on its direction, localization, and differential coupling to the initial and transition states.
